headline: In Steady Disruption, factory machine operators prepare for changing schedules first and possible lost physical shifts later.
whatTheySay: **Planning and paperwork** may move to AI before robots handle factory materials.
Operators ask for **written staffing terms** and paid, supervised practice before new controls change their work.
Some welcome **proven tools** but still want physical samples and guards checked.
whatTheyThink: A later **robot or camera** could reduce operator places even if thinking AI first changes the office.
New schedules could cut **setup time or premiums** before a machine replaces the full job.
Some see **new technical skills** as a route forward; others see a partner’s desk income exposed first.
howTheyFeel: **144 of 202** are anxious in Steady Disruption, often because their own or household paid hours could shrink.
**48 of 202** are uneasy while work still pays and changes remain gradual.
Only **10 of 202** are calm; all are early-stage workers in this reviewed set.

differences.text: Average worry is 3.00 for 40 late-stage profiles and 2.30 for 81 early-stage profiles (1 calm to 5 panicked).
Thin-cushion profiles average 2.85 worry (72), versus 2.44 among strong-cushion profiles (63).
Change-job appears in 29 of 40 late-stage profiles and 13 of 81 early-stage profiles, each a conditional plan rather than a confirmed move.

least.name: Early workers with room
least.story: All ten calm profiles are early-stage; nine are adaptive and nine have at least a month saved while their present work remains paid.

most.name: Paid hours at risk
most.story: The 144 anxious profiles span every life stage and cushion, with possible cuts to machine shifts, premiums or a partner’s income.

whatTheyDo.text: 105 of 202 plan AI learning; Nora would enrol in an alarm-log course if offered a funded, paid, guarded place.
97 of 202 plan retraining; Fatima Dubois would take a colour-change course if offered paid, guarded, fitter-led practice.
88 of 202 consider a job change; Carlos Evans would apply after lost shifts if a posted local kiln job is safe and its net base pay fits.
71 of 202 wait for evidence; Fatima compares a posted evening rota and premium with three pay slips.
65 of 202 act together; Freya Haddad takes three die-booking errors to a joint union safety meeting.

quotes.name: Karl Patel
quotes.text: A robot should mean a shorter week, not a smaller team.

quotes.name: Colin Reyes
quotes.text: An empty place on the rota is still a person missing at the break table.

quotes.name: Fatima Dubois
quotes.text: The loom cannot pay a premium for a shift that disappears.

thoughts.text: Factory automation could shrink operator places or paid shifts.
New software or production changes could shrink paid roles or hours.
My own paid work may remain intact at first.
New machine or software skills could determine my next role.
My partner's job could shrink before or alongside mine.
